jsonld.headline: Just wrapped up Chainguard #Assemble2026 in NYC.
jsonld.articleBody:
Just wrapped up Chainguard #Assemble2026 in NYC. Still processing this one.

I walked into rooms with CISOs, engineers, and security leaders from companies like Cisco, Amazon Web Services (AWS), OpenAI, KKR, etc.

Grateful to the Chainguard team (especially Katie Kern) for creating space for me to be in those conversations.

What made this experience different wasn’t just the talks. It was seeing how seriously the industry is rethinking the foundation of software in the age of AI.

A few things that stuck with me:

1. AI is accelerating everything and expanding the attack surface: More code. More dependencies. More risk.
2. The shift is from writing code to trusting what’s running in production: This showed up everywhere, from CI/CD to agent workflows.
3. Secure-by-default is becoming the baseline: Not a feature, the foundation. 

You could see it in everything Chainguard announced.
AI agents are becoming a new class of dependency, and most teams are not yet ready for it.

The thing that surprised me most was that the conversations were not about moving faster; they were about moving fast without losing trust. That changed how I think about everything I am building right now.

Between working on authentication infrastructure and building Splita, the takeaway is simple:
You cannot bolt on trust later; it has to be built into the system.

I appreciate everyone who took the time to share insights and push my thinking. This is one of those rooms I know I will come back to.

Are we building systems we actually understand anymore?

Some great conversations by people building this future in real time:
Dan Lorenc (secure-by-default infrastructure + software supply chain)
Patrick Donahue (scaling trust across the SDLC)
Ram Ramani (why security has to start at the model level)
David Stern (limits of AI vs human judgment in security)
Dwayne McDaniel (software supply chain + secrets security)

Appreciate all the insights 🙏
